programme_review.finding: Projection/cosine definition, orthonormal coordinate formula and choice of product method are in scope. The dimension-n passage remains explicitly labelled as an approfondissement; no official atom changed.

independent_scientific_reasoning: For nonzero vectors, positive norms times a real cosine define a real scalar. Angles are now restricted to the nonzero case before the formula is printed; the zero-vector convention is separate. Same/opposite direction give cos=1/-1, orthogonality gives cos=0, and u·u=||u||². The value is independent of the representative of an oriented angle because cosine is 2π-periodic.

For projection, place the common origin at O, let A represent u and B represent v, orient OA towards A. In orthonormal coordinates adapted to this direction, u=(r,0) with r>0 and v=(tr,h), H=(tr,0). The signed length OH is tr, not |tr|. Therefore ||u|| times signed OH equals r²t=u·v for every real t,h. This includes projections behind O, at O, ahead of O, and v=0. The zero first vector is excluded because it would not define the line OA; its product is already defined as zero.

Bilinearity in an orthonormal base gives x1x2+y1y2. The visible numeric example gives 3×2+(−1)×5=1 and the angle example gives 4×3×cos(π/3)=6. The analytic oracle examples give 11 and 0 respectively. In an oblique basis i=(1,0), j=(1,1), i·j=1 whereas the naive coordinate dot of their basis coordinates would be 0; this independently verifies the warning about a nonorthonormal base.
The higher-dimensional displayed sum defines the standard Euclidean product on R^n and is explicitly labelled optional; no argument depends on treating it as a Première requirement.

programme_review.finding: Transformation of MA·MB and demonstration of its zero locus are expressly in scope. The missing scientific content was repaired using the current official programme, with no invented atom or scope reduction.

independent_scientific_reasoning: Let A≠B and I be their midpoint. In a translated/rotated orthonormal frame A=(0,0), B=(2a,0), a>0, M=(x,y), MA²−MB²=4a(x−a)=2 IM·AB. Equal nonnegative distances are therefore equivalent to IM·AB=0. Also MA·AB=−2ax, so its value on the bisector x=a is −2a²=−AB²/2. This is a general proof, not a numeric sample; the coordinate-free expansion is now printed in the source.

With MA=MI−AB/2 and MB=MI+AB/2, bilinearity and symmetry cancel the mixed terms: MA·MB=MI²−AB²/4. Its zero locus is the circle with center I and radius AB/2, including A and B. This differs from the bisector. M=I is on the bisector but gives MA·MB=−AB²/4, not zero. The independent polarization equality is universally true and cannot characterize the bisector.

The old iff with the polarization identity was refuted by A=(0,0), B=(2,0), M=A: the identity holds but MA≠MB. M=(1,0) refutes both the former positive-half MA·AB condition and the former zero MA·MB characterization. All three faulty claims now have direct source-facing regression tests and symbolic identities.

For a nonflat triangle, H∈(BC) and AH·BC=0 uniquely determine the altitude foot, since H=B+t(C−B) gives t=((A−B)·(C−B))/||C−B||² and B≠C. H need not lie on segment BC, which is why the line is explicitly used.

Area is half a base times the corresponding height: AB×AC×|sin(A)|/2. The interior angle lies in (0,π), so sin(A)>0 and is the positive square root of 1−cos²(A). For A=(0,0), B=(4,0), C=(1,3), AB·AC=4, the norms are 4 and sqrt(10), cosine=1/sqrt(10), sine=3/sqrt(10), and area=6 square units. This agrees independently with base 4 and height 3.

reasoning: Take u=(r,0), r>0 and v=(s,t) in an adapted orthonormal frame. Projection has signed length s, so r*s equals u dot v even for s<0 and v=0. u=0 is separately defined and cannot define the projection line. Cosine of an oriented angle is representative-independent. Both numeric examples give1 and6.

MA=MI-AB/2 and MB=MI+AB/2. Squaring and subtracting gives -2MI dot AB=2IM dot AB. Also MA dot AB=-IM dot AB-AB²/2; the negative sign is necessary. Equality of nonnegative distances is equivalent to equality of squares. A!=B defines the unique bisector.

Multiplying the same vector decompositions cancels mixed terms and gives MA dot MB=MI²-AB²/4. Its zero set is exactly the circle of center I, radius AB/2, including A and B. M=I refutes the old bisector/circle confusion, and M=A refutes the old universal-identity iff.

For a nonflat triangle BC is nonzero. H=B+t(C-B) and AH dot BC=0 give one real t; the foot is on the supporting line, not necessarily the segment. Base times perpendicular height over2 gives the printed area formula. The interior angle lies in(0,pi), so the positive sine branch is justified; the coordinate example independently has base4, height3, area6.

Canonical mutations test both signs, signed projection and an imaginary term that vanishes at0 andpi/2. The realness assertion now excludes that false scalar. General symbolic identities supplement the printed proofs; finite examples are not used as proofs of general statements.
